clue.text: The best bet? Back silver, in the view of a non-believer

indicators.note: being in the view of something here means sitting inside it, so silver is placed within
Back tells us to read the tipster's word from right to left

parts.note: a nap is a racing tipster's most confident selection of the day
Ag is the chemical symbol for silver

explanation.surface: A punter backing a horse to place, which a sceptic thinks is the best wager.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' reverses the bet and 'in the view of' puts silver inside. A nap is British racing slang for a tipster's strongest pick of the day.
explanation.definitionFit: A pagan is someone outside the main religions, so a heathen or unbeliever.

clue.text: Provide initial cover

annotationWithheld.why: Provide initial cover (6): TENDER fits 'Provide' (tender = offer), but no sense of tender for 'initial cover' could be found or confirmed by search, so the second half cannot be explained honestly.

clue.text: Any Spode can be put out for special occasions

indicators.note: china put out on a table is set out in a new order, so these letters get rearranged

explanation.surface: Fine Spode china is brought out for celebrations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can be put out' shuffles ANYSPODE into OPEN DAYS. Spode is a famous English pottery brand.
explanation.definitionFit: Open days are events when institutions welcome the public, so particular occasions.

clue.text: Unusually frantic break

indicators.note: doing something unusually means in a strange way, so the letters are reworked

explanation.surface: An extraordinarily hectic holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unusually' rearranges FRANTIC into INFRACT; 'break' reads as a rest but is a verb here.
explanation.definitionFit: To infract a rule is to violate or breach it.

clue.text: Blisters make for Bank Holiday blues

parts.note: Whit Monday was a British public holiday after Whitsun
lows are moods of depression, the blues

explanation.surface: A public holiday leaves people feeling gloomy and sore.
explanation.walkthrough: Whit Monday is the British bank holiday after Whitsun (Pentecost); 'make for' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A whitlow is a painful swelling or abscess near a fingernail, loosely a blister.

clue.text: Single copyright held by gallery chief doesn't become diminished

indicators.note: being held by the gallery means sitting inside its name

parts.note: the Tate is a London art gallery
a single is one run in cricket

indicators.note: chief means the leading letter of the following word

explanation.surface: A gallery head's single copyright claim fails to shrink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'held by' puts the single and copyright inside the gallery, and 'chief' takes the first letter of 'doesn't'; 'become' is a link. The Tate is a London gallery; a single is one run in cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: Something truncated has been cut short, made smaller.

clue.text: Nails wayward sleeping partner without regret

indicators.note: wayward letters stray from their places, so the phrase is rearranged after the second word is taken out

explanation.surface: A business partner who has gone astray feels no remorse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' marks REGRET taken out of the letters of SLEEPING PARTNER; 'wayward' rearranges the remaining SLEPINPAN into PANEL PINS.
explanation.definitionFit: Panel pins are small slim nails used for fixing thin boards.

clue.text: About to let fly at ill-mannered person

parts.note: C is short for circa, about
to hurl is to throw hard, let fly

explanation.surface: Someone throws things at a rude person.
explanation.definitionFit: A churl is a boorish, rude individual.

clue.text: Slight change to rules to exclude Spain

indicators.note: a change to something alters it, so these letters are reordered
to exclude a letter is to leave it out of the result

parts.note: E is the international vehicle code for Spain

explanation.surface: A minor amendment to regulations keeps Spain out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'change to' rearranges RULES, and 'to exclude' removes E (Spain), leaving SLUR.
explanation.definitionFit: A slur is an insult, as is a slight.

clue.text: Forest in Germany he wants to cultivate?

indicators.note: in places the forest inside the country's abbreviation

parts.note: the Forest of Arden is a woodland in Warwickshire, setting of As You Like It

explanation.surface: A German who wants to grow a forest.
explanation.walkthrough: ARDEN, the English forest of Shakespeare's As You Like It, goes 'in' GER. The definition is cryptic: a gardener is one who wants to cultivate.
explanation.definitionFit: A gardener is a person who tends and grows plants, someone wishing to till.

clue.text: Catalogue number in Italy to be updated

indicators.note: updating a list rearranges its contents, so these letters move

explanation.surface: An Italian product number that needs revising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be updated' rearranges N and ITALY into LITANY; 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A litany is a long tedious list, a catalogue of items.

clue.text: 27 discovered during Majorcan holiday

indicators.note: found within the words, so the letters sit inside the phrase

explanation.surface: Something found while on a Spanish island break.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer to 27 (WHALE) defines it; the letters sit inside majORCAn.
explanation.definitionFit: The orca, or killer whale, is a large toothed whale.

clue.text: Enclosure holding naval man, an NCO

indicators.note: holding means the first piece wraps round the second

parts.note: a corral is a pen for livestock
PO stands for petty officer in the navy

explanation.surface: A pen containing a sailor, who is a non-commissioned officer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'holding' signals a container: the sailor sits inside the livestock pen.
explanation.definitionFit: A corporal is a non-commissioned officer rank in the army.

clue.text: Attention given to calculating 50 + 999 + 8 — 50

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty

indicators.note: calculating works the figures over, so the letters they give are juggled

parts.note: IM is a loose Roman way of writing one less than a thousand
eight is the figure spelt out
L again is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: Getting noticed for doing sums.
explanation.walkthrough: 'calculating' rearranges L, IM, EIGHT and L into LIMELIGHT; the plus and minus signs are decoration. IM for 999 is not strict Roman notation.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in the limelight means being the focus of public notice.

clue.text: Fancy maintaining politician one sees as wet!

indicators.note: maintaining means holding, so the first piece contains the second

parts.note: to fancy is to wish for
MP is a Member of Parliament
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Someone dreaming of a politician that strikes them as feeble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'maintaining' signals a container; 'sees as' is a link. Wet is British slang for feeble, weak-willed.
explanation.definitionFit: Wet in British usage means feeble or weak, just as wimpish does.

clue.text: He drew the line at being overweight!

definitions.text: He drew the line at being overweight!

parts.words: He drew the line at being overweight!
parts.note: the man behind the load-line painted on ships' hulls to stop them being dangerously overloaded

explanation.surface: Someone who refused to tolerate getting fat.
explanation.walkthrough: Samuel Plimsoll, a British MP, campaigned for the load line on ships; 'drew the line' and 'overweight' look like a diet story.
explanation.definitionFit: Samuel Plimsoll introduced the mark showing the safe loading limit of a ship.

clue.text: Settled back in outhouse, hidden from view

indicators.note: in places the turned word inside the outhouse

parts.note: a shed is an outbuilding

indicators.note: back says the word for settled is read in the reverse direction

parts.note: sat means settled or perched

explanation.surface: Someone sat in a garden shed, out of sight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns SAT into TAS, which goes 'in' SHED.
explanation.definitionFit: Stashed means stored away secretly, concealed.

clue.text: Shrewd motoring organisation involved in backing for public transport

indicators.note: backing means the combined result is read from end to start
involved in means the organisation is set inside the adjective

parts.note: smart means shrewd or clever
the RAC, Royal Automobile Club, is a British motoring organisation

explanation.surface: A clever motoring body supports public transport.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involved in' puts RAC into SMART making SRACMART, and 'backing' reverses the lot. The RAC is a British breakdown service; 'for' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Tramcars are street railway vehicles carrying passengers on public routes.

clue.text: Stored furniture is in outermost shed

indicators.note: is in tells us the furniture sits inside the other letters
outermost means the first and last letters

parts.note: a table is an item of furniture

explanation.surface: Furniture kept in the very edge of a shed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outermost' takes S and D from 'shed', and TABLE 'is in' them.
explanation.definitionFit: Stabled means kept or housed, as horses are in stables.

clue.text: Ashamed to open it — enthralled by what's inside

indicators.note: what's inside the words is the string of letters within them

explanation.surface: Feeling guilty about opening something and being gripped by the contents.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run inside oPEN IT ENThralled; 'to' and 'enthralled by' lead you to look for a container.
explanation.definitionFit: Penitent means feeling regret for wrongdoing, contrite.

clue.text: Wind up topless with nonchalance!

indicators.note: topless means the first letter is removed

parts.note: to wind up is British slang for to tease

explanation.surface: Teasing someone casually while bare-chested.
explanation.walkthrough: 'topless' drops the T of TEASE. Wind up is British slang for tease.
explanation.definitionFit: Ease means relaxed naturalness, nonchalance.

clue.text: Talked about members' donations

indicators.note: talked about means said aloud, so we want a word that sounds alike

parts.note: arms are limbs, members of the body

explanation.surface: People discussed what the club members gave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Talked about' signals the sound match: in non-rhotic British speech ARMS sounds like ALMS.
explanation.definitionFit: Alms are gifts of money or food to the poor.

clue.text: Vegetable essence

definitions.meaning: a large green squash grown in British gardens
the innermost core or vital part of something

explanation.definitionFit: Marrow is both a vegetable of the squash family and the innermost core of things.

clue.text: Dogsbody initially given orders from queen

indicators.note: initially means take the first letter of each word

parts.note: ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the queen

explanation.surface: A servant first given instructions by the queen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initially' takes G, O, F from 'given orders from', and ER is added.
explanation.definitionFit: A gofer is a junior who runs errands, a dogsbody.

clue.text: Overlooks young women

definitions.meaning: girls, unmarried ladies addressed by a title

explanation.definitionFit: To miss is to fail to notice, and Misses are young unmarried women.

clue.text: Second African returning to support operation

parts.note: to second a proposal is to back it

indicators.note: returning means the word for the African goes in reverse

parts.note: a Moor is a North African

explanation.surface: An African's second trip home helps an operation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second' is a verb meaning back; 'returning' turns MOOR into ROOM; 'to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Backroom staff do behind-the-scenes support work for an organisation.

clue.text: 12 describes what a great time we're having!

definitions.meaning: the answer to 12 across, the killer sea mammal

definitions.text: describes what a great time we're having!
definitions.meaning: the idiom of having a wonderful time uses this word

explanation.surface: Someone enjoying themselves greatly.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half alludes to the idiom 'having a whale of a time'.
explanation.definitionFit: A killer whale is a whale, and 'a whale of a time' means a wonderful time.

clue.text: Suitcases found in cars?

parts.note: read gear as luggage, so containers for luggage in a vehicle, but really the transmission housing

explanation.surface: Luggage stowed in a car boot.
explanation.walkthrough: Gear can mean luggage, so suitcases are boxes for gear; really this is the housing of a car's transmission.
explanation.definitionFit: A gearbox is the casing holding a vehicle's gears.
